problem: Vision-language navigation had grown into many heterogeneous tasks (R2R, REVERIE, ALFRED, EQA, Touchdown, CVDN, HANNA, ...) with no dedicated review, and no principled way to categorize them. Grouping by visual input or simulator does not work: e.g. R2R and REVERIE share the Matterport3D Simulator but differ in task setting. Prior surveys covered only embodied AI broadly, vision-language multimodality, or classical robot navigation.
motivation: VLN models and datasets were being released very quickly, so researchers needed a map of the tasks, their metrics, typical methods and open limitations. The driving observation is that visual input is similar within indoor tasks (homes) and within outdoor tasks (street scenes). What really distinguishes tasks is the language: whether instructions come once or over several turns, whether they describe a goal or a route, and whether the agent may ask questions.
key_idea: Classify VLN tasks by the characteristics of their language instructions: single-turn tasks are either goal-oriented or route-oriented, and multi-turn tasks are either passive or interactive; each task is then reviewed by definition, metrics and typical methods.
insight: The instruction form determines the capabilities a task demands and so shapes model design. Goal-oriented tasks (REVERIE, ALFRED, EQA, RoomNav) need self-planning, exploration and grounding of goal objects. Route-oriented tasks (R2R and variants, Touchdown) need step-by-step alignment of instruction to trajectory. Multi-turn tasks (CVDN/NDH, HANNA, VNLA, Talk The Walk) need dialog-history memory and deciding when to ask. From the compiled R2R test-unseen leaderboard (single run), the survey concludes that combining a pre-trained VLN backbone with data augmentation works best (REM on VLN↻BERT: SR 0.65, SPL 0.59); pre-exploration and beam search inflate SR at large TL cost. There are no ablations, since this is a survey.
method: Taxonomy (Table 1): tasks split into single-turn (goal-oriented: LANI, ALFRED, Talk2Car, XWORLD, 3D Doom, Visual Semantic Navigation, EQA, RoomNav, REVERIE, Behavioral Robot Navigation, SUNCG nav; route-oriented: R2R, R4R, RxR, R6R/R8R, R2R-CE, XL-R2R, Touchdown, RUN, StreetNav, StreetLearn, ARRAMON) and multi-turn (passive: CEREALBAR, VNLA, HANNA; interactive: CVDN, Just Ask, Talk The Walk, RobotSlang); also flags outdoor settings and compound sub-tasks (manipulation M / question answering Q / localization L).

Datasets & simulators review (Table 2): covers SUNCG, Matterport3D, 2D-3D-S and Replica, plus simulators LANI, AI2-THOR, VizDoom, Gibson, House3D, Matterport3D Simulator and Habitat, with observation type and 2D/3D.

Goal-oriented task review: gives task definition, metrics (ALFRED Task/Goal-Condition success with path weighting; EQA d_T/d_Δ/d_min, %r_T, %stop; REVERIE RGS-style success within 3 m) and typical methods (LingUNet, SuReAL, Seq2Seq+progress monitor, MOCA, PACMAN/NMC, BRM, REVERIE navigator-pointer-interaction model, GCN prior knowledge).

Route-oriented review: covers R2R metrics (SR, NE, PL/TL, SPL, ONE, OSR, nDTW, CLS, instruction-fidelity metrics). R2R methods are sorted into 7 classes: exploration strategy, beyond-Seq2Seq architectures, RL+IL (with the combined loss L = λ L_IL + L_RL), language grounding, data augmentation, pre-training, and other work (sim-to-real, diagnostics).
R2R leaderboard compilation (Table 3): collects test-unseen results of about 27 published methods under Single Run, Pre-explore and Beam Search settings (NE/OR/SR/SPL, TL).

R2R variants and outdoor tasks: surveys R4R/R6R/R8R, VLN-CE (topological-map modular approach, meta-learning for camera configurations), RxR, XL-R2R, Touchdown (Learning-to-Stop, style-transfer augmentation), StreetLearn/StreetNav, Talk2Nav, RUN and ARRAMON.

Multi-turn review and outlook: covers CEREALBAR, HANNA, VNLA/ASKNAV, Talk The Walk (MASC), CVDN/NDH (CMN, RMM), Just Ask and RobotSlang. Then discusses limitations (poor generalization, lack of high-quality data, weak interactivity) and opportunities (algorithmic, external-knowledge and cognitive-architecture knowledge; sim-to-real; lightweight models).

setting.observation: n/a (covers panoramic RGB on nav-graphs, egocentric RGB-D in House3D/Habitat/AI2-THOR, Street View panoramas, 2D grid worlds)
setting.action_space: n/a (covers discrete nav-graph viewpoints, low-level discrete moves, continuous quadcopter control)
setting.simulator: n/a (reviews Matterport3D Simulator, Habitat, House3D, AI2-THOR, VizDoom, Gibson, LANI/Unity, AirSim, Google Street View)

numbers_note: Survey paper with no own method, so no own results. Table 3 is a compiled R2R test-unseen leaderboard of other methods (Single Run / Pre-explore / Beam Search), e.g. REM on VLN↻BERT with NE 3.87, SR 0.65, SPL 0.59. Several of its entries look like transcription errors and should not be reused as sources: Seq2Seq NE listed as 20.4; Regretful Agent has SR 0.56 > OR 0.48, apparently swapped; PREVALENT duplicates PRESS's row (4.53/0.57/0.53). Take numbers from the original papers instead.
results: No new experimental results. The survey's compiled R2R test-unseen leaderboard identifies REM (Random Environmental Mixup on VLN↻BERT) as the single-run state of the art (NE 3.87, SR 0.65, SPL 0.59), ahead of VLN↻BERT (SR 0.63, SPL 0.57) and NvEM (SR 0.58, SPL 0.54). Active Exploration leads under pre-exploration (SR 0.70, SPL 0.68), and AuxRN leads beam search by SPL (0.21).
limitations: It is a descriptive taxonomy only, with no quantitative cross-task analysis. Coverage stops around mid-2021: no VLN-CE/RxR/REVERIE leaderboards and no LLM-era methods.

The compiled R2R leaderboard contains apparent transcription errors (Seq2Seq NE 20.4; Regretful SR/OR swapped; PREVALENT row copies PRESS). Several factual slips also appear: EQA described as the agent 'asking' a question, PRESS said to use GPT-3, BERT cited to the Transformer paper.
Some category boundaries are fuzzy: the 'passive' multi-turn group includes HANNA/VNLA, where the agent can request help, and Touchdown/StreetLearn/StreetNav are only superficially distinguished.
